 By Legis1 Editorial · Edited by Matthew Dougherty Tuesday, November 17, 2026 · 3 min read Why It Matters
 Federal student loan borrowers face tighter borrowing limits and fewer repayment options under changes that took effect July 1, according to a new Congressional Research Service (CRS) report . The changes create different rules depending on when loans were issued, complicating repayment decisions for millions of borrowers. ​ 
 The Department of Education projects $83.6 billion in new Direct Loans for fiscal 2027, underscoring the federal lending program's reach as Congress considers further changes to student loan policy. The new rules also affect existing borrowers who take out additional loans. According to CRS, borrowers with loans issued before July 1 who receive a new Direct Loan on or after that date become subject to a narrower selection of repayment plans for all their Direct Loans.
 The Big Picture
 The William D. Ford Federal Direct Loan program is the nation's largest source of federal financial assistance for higher education. According to CRS, approximately $1.6 trillion in principal and interest remained outstanding at the end of the third quarter of fiscal 2026, representing loans borrowed by or on behalf of 38.3 million people.
 Many of the changes stem from H.R. 1 , the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, sponsored by Rep. Jodey Arrington (R-TX) and signed into law July 4, 2025. The law eliminated graduate PLUS loans for new borrowers beginning July 1, while allowing certain previously enrolled students to continue borrowing under transitional rules. It also established a $257,500 lifetime borrowing limit for students, subject to statutory exclusions and exceptions.
 The legislation substantially narrowed repayment options for borrowers taking out new loans. Those borrowers generally must choose between the Tiered Standard repayment plan, which requires fixed payments over a period determined by the amount owed, and the income-driven Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP). Under the new system, borrowers with larger balances could remain in repayment for decades. The Tiered Standard plan offers repayment periods of 10 to 25 years, while RAP can extend repayment for up to 30 years.
 The law also repeals statutory authority for the Income-Contingent Repayment (ICR) and Pay As You Earn (PAYE) plans effective July 1, 2028, requiring affected borrowers to transition to other repayment options. The Department of Education is implementing the changes amid legal challenges over which graduate programs qualify for higher federal borrowing limits.
 Advertisement 
 Regulations issued June 9 further defined the term "professional student," which determines eligibility for certain graduate borrowing limits. A federal court preliminarily stayed part of that definition June 24 in American Association of Nurse Practitioners v. McMahon . A second court issued a preliminary injunction Oct. 16 in Association of Accredited Naturopathic Colleges v. McMahon , requiring the department to recognize certain health professions programs as professional degrees while litigation continues.
 The department later published an interim list of qualifying programs, warning that the classifications could change depending on the litigation's outcome. The administration is also dismantling the Saving on a Valuable Education (SAVE) repayment plan. A federal court vacated the program's regulations March 10 in Missouri v. Trump , and the Education Department announced next steps March 27 to move affected borrowers into other repayment plans. Federal loan servicers have confirmed that the SAVE plan ended following the court order.
 The Bottom Line
 Federal student loan borrowers face another deadline Dec. 31, when enrollment closes for a temporary discount on the automatic payment interest rate. Under the temporary interest rate reduction , eligible borrowers enrolled in automatic payments receive a 1-percentage-point reduction in their loan interest rates, up from the previous 0.25-percentage-point discount. The enhanced benefit is scheduled to remain available through June 30, 2028.
 Meanwhile, legal challenges over professional-degree classifications could alter borrowing eligibility for some graduate students, and borrowers enrolled in ICR or PAYE face a July 1, 2028, deadline to transition to another repayment plan. The changes leave millions of borrowers navigating different borrowing limits, repayment options, and eligibility requirements based on when their loans were issued.
